_doc: Curated 'about this song/artist' blurbs shown in the card's About section. Keys are normalized artist names (lowercase, diacritics stripped, non-alphanumerics collapsed to single spaces — see normKey in lib/stories.ts). A more specific 'country|genre|artist' key wins over a plain artist key. Values are short grounded prose (2–3 sentences max) — cite era/place/genre facts, no invented history. Populated by scripts/enrich-stories.ts and by hand.
ghana|disco|george darko: George Darko pioneered 'burger highlife' in early-1980s West Berlin — Ghanaian highlife guitar over synth-funk and disco grooves, made by and for the Ghanaian diaspora. His 1983 hit 'Akoo Te Brofo' defined the style.
nazia hassan: Karachi-born Nazia Hassan became South Asia's first pop superstar at 15 with 'Aap Jaisa Koi' (1980), then made 'Disco Deewane' with producer Biddu — a disco record that topped charts from Pakistan to Brazil.
fazil say: Fazıl Say is Turkey's most celebrated concert pianist and composer, equally known for Beethoven cycles and works that fold Anatolian folk modes into Western classical forms.
kourosh yaghmaei: Kourosh Yaghmaei is the godfather of Iranian psychedelic rock — his fuzz-drenched 1970s singles like 'Gol-e Yakh' circulated underground for decades after the 1979 revolution pushed his music out of official channels.
lisa ono: Lisa Ono, born in São Paulo and raised in Tokyo, is the best-known voice of Japanese bossa nova — she has recorded with Antônio Carlos Jobim's circle and made bossa a fixture of Japanese café culture since 1989.
minyo crusaders: Minyo Crusaders rework Japanese min'yō folk songs — fishermen's and farmers' work songs — over cumbia, ska and Afro-Cuban rhythms, a ten-piece band from Fussa that made traditional Japan danceable again.
steve monite: Steve Monite's 'Only You' (1984) is the crown jewel of Nigerian boogie — Lagos disco-funk pressed in tiny quantities, rediscovered by collectors and reissued to global acclaim three decades later.
sattas: Sattas are Istanbul's flagship reggae band, singing roots reggae in Turkish since 2007 and proving the genre could take hold on the Bosphorus.
lucky dube: Lucky Dube was South Africa's biggest reggae star — he switched from mbaqanga to reggae in 1984 under apartheid, and albums like 'Slave' made him one of Africa's best-selling artists ever.
tatsuro yamashita: Tatsuro Yamashita is the king of Japanese city pop — the polished, disco-and-boogie-inflected sound of 1980s bubble-era Tokyo that found a second global life through online crate-digging.
fela kuti: Fela Kuti invented Afrobeat in 1970s Lagos — James Brown funk fused with Yoruba rhythms and jazz horns, stretched into hypnotic 15-minute political sermons aimed squarely at Nigeria's military governments.
tony allen: Tony Allen was Fela Kuti's drummer and Afrobeat's co-architect — Fela said that 'without Tony Allen, there would be no Afrobeat.'
william onyeabor: William Onyeabor self-released eight albums of visionary synth-funk from his own pressing plant in Enugu between 1977 and 1985, then became a born-again Christian and refused to discuss his music for the rest of his life.
king sunny ade: King Sunny Adé is the king of jùjú — Lagos dance music of talking drums and glittering interlocking guitars — and one of the first African artists marketed worldwide as a global star.
burna boy: Burna Boy calls his sound Afro-fusion — Port Harcourt-born, he won the 2021 Grammy for Best Global Music Album with 'Twice as Tall'.
niniola: Niniola is the queen of afro-house — her Lagos-meets-Johannesburg dance records made her one of the first Nigerian artists to chart on Billboard's dance charts.
sarz: Sarz is one of Nigeria's defining producers — the beat architect behind hits for Wizkid and Burna Boy who helped shape the modern Afrobeats sound.
ebo taylor: Ebo Taylor has been the guitarist-arranger spine of Ghanaian highlife since the 1950s; he studied in London alongside Fela Kuti and folded funk and Afrobeat into the Fante highlife tradition.
ata kak: Ata Kak's homemade 1994 tape 'Obaa Sima' — frantic Twi rap over lo-fi house beats — sold almost nothing, until Awesome Tapes From Africa rediscovered it and made him a global cult figure two decades later.
osibisa: Osibisa, formed in London in 1969 by Ghanaian and Caribbean musicians, took Afro-rock to the world's stadiums — their sound was famously described as 'criss-cross rhythms that explode with happiness'.
pat thomas: Pat Thomas, 'the Golden Voice of Africa', has sung Ghanaian highlife since the 1960s and fronted the burger-highlife wave from Berlin in the 1980s.
nusrat fateh ali khan: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan took qawwali — Sufi devotional song from the shrines of Punjab — to the entire planet, improvising ecstatic vocal flights over handclaps and harmonium for hours at a stretch.
abida parveen: Abida Parveen is Sufi music's reigning voice — a woman singing a tradition long dominated by men, carrying the poetry of Shah Abdul Latif and Bulleh Shah.
atif aslam: Atif Aslam went from Lahore rock band Jal to becoming South Asia's most streamed playback voice.
selda bagcan: Selda Bağcan sang Anatolian protest folk over fuzz guitar in the 1970s, was jailed repeatedly after the 1980 coup, and decades later became one of the most sampled voices in international hip hop.
erkin koray: Erkin Koray plugged the electric guitar into Turkish music — his 1974 'Elektronik Türküler' is the cornerstone of Anatolian psychedelia.
baris manco: Barış Manço was Anatolian rock's flamboyant prince — 200-odd songs and a beloved TV show that made him a household name across Turkey.
sezen aksu: Sezen Aksu is 'the Little Sparrow' — the songwriter-queen of Turkish pop who wrote the songs that made Tarkan a global star.
tarkan: Tarkan's 1997 hit 'Şımarık' — the kiss-kiss song — carried Turkish pop farther abroad than any record before it.
ajda pekkan: Ajda Pekkan is Turkey's 'Superstar' — the diva who wrapped Turkish pop in French chanson glamour and 1970s disco strings.
zeki muren: Zeki Müren, 'the Sun of Art Music', was Turkey's most beloved classical voice — a flamboyant, gender-bending icon adored across every social divide.
googoosh: Googoosh was pre-revolution Iran's biggest star; silenced at home after 1979, she stayed, said nothing for 21 years, then returned to sold-out world tours in 2000.
mohammad reza shajarian: Mohammad-Reza Shajarian was the supreme master of Persian classical singing — when he died in 2020, crowds sang his banned anthem 'Morgh-e Sahar' outside the hospital.
kayhan kalhor: Kayhan Kalhor made the kamancheh — the Persian spiked fiddle — a world-stage instrument, including with Yo-Yo Ma's Silk Road Ensemble.
mariya takeuchi: Mariya Takeuchi's 'Plastic Love' (1984) became city pop's accidental global anthem when YouTube's algorithm resurrected it three decades after release.
sadao watanabe: Sadao Watanabe is the elder statesman of Japanese jazz — the Tokyo saxophonist who brought bossa nova back from Brazil to Japan in the 1960s.
toshiko akiyoshi: Toshiko Akiyoshi went from Beppu to leading one of jazz's great big bands in New York, writing Ellington-scale suites voiced with Japanese instruments and themes.
joao gilberto: João Gilberto invented the bossa nova guitar beat in a Bahia bathroom — his whispered 1958 'Chega de Saudade' started the genre.
antonio carlos jobim: Antônio Carlos Jobim wrote the bossa nova songbook — 'The Girl from Ipanema', 'Corcovado', 'Águas de Março' — from Rio's Ipanema neighborhood.
gilberto gil: Gilberto Gil co-founded Tropicália, was jailed and exiled by Brazil's dictatorship, and decades later served as the country's Minister of Culture.
caetano veloso: Caetano Veloso is Tropicália's poet — exiled to London by the dictatorship in 1969, he came home to become Brazil's most influential songwriter.
milton nascimento: Milton Nascimento's otherworldly falsetto and the Clube da Esquina collective put Minas Gerais on the map of world music.
heitor villa lobos: Villa-Lobos folded Brazil's folk melodies into concert music — his Bachianas Brasileiras imagine Bach reborn in Rio.
ratos de porao: Ratos de Porão have been São Paulo's hardcore-punk conscience since 1981, chronicling Brazil's crises at breakneck speed.
astor piazzolla: Astor Piazzolla scandalized Buenos Aires by dragging tango into the concert hall — his nuevo tango put the bandoneón through fugues, jazz and dissonance.
mercedes sosa: Mercedes Sosa, 'the voice of Latin America', sang the nueva canción of the continent's struggles and was forced into exile by Argentina's junta.
soda stereo: Soda Stereo are Spanish-language rock's Beatles — the Buenos Aires trio whose 1980s records made rock en español a continental language.
gilda: Gilda left teaching to sing cumbia and died in a 1996 bus crash at 34 — Argentina turned her into a popular saint, with shrines along the highway where she died.
damas gratis: Damas Gratis invented cumbia villera — the raw keyboard cumbia of Buenos Aires' barrios — and made it the sound of the Argentine street.
gotan project: Gotan Project, formed in Paris in 1999, spliced Buenos Aires tango with downtempo electronics and made bandoneón club music.
edith piaf: Édith Piaf rose from singing on Pigalle street corners to embodying French chanson itself — 'La Vie en rose' and 'Non, je ne regrette rien' are national monuments.
serge gainsbourg: Serge Gainsbourg spent four decades scandalizing and seducing France, hopping from jazz to yé-yé to reggae to the lush pop of 'Histoire de Melody Nelson'.
daft punk: Daft Punk turned Parisian house music into robot mythology — 'the French touch' that conquered global pop before the duo vanished in 2021.
cerrone: Cerrone's 'Supernature' (1977) is Euro-disco's cosmic peak — the French drummer-producer's four-on-the-floor records prefigured house music.
nouvelle vague: Nouvelle Vague's name is the joke and the thesis: 'new wave' in French is 'bossa nova' in Portuguese — so they cover post-punk classics as whispered Brazilian lounge.
berurier noir: Bérurier Noir were 1980s French punk's beating heart — drum machine, saxophone and anti-fascist singalongs that filled halls with 'la jeunesse emmerde le Front National'.
amalia rodrigues: Amália Rodrigues is fado — the Lisbon singer who made saudade, the untranslatable Portuguese ache, a world emotion.
xutos pontapes: Xutos & Pontapés have been Portugal's rock institution since 1978 — born of the punk wave that followed the Carnation Revolution.
richie campbell: Richie Campbell built a Lisbon reggae and dancehall scene big enough to headline arenas — a Portuguese artist singing Jamaican styles on his own terms.
frederic chopin: Chopin left Warsaw at 20 with a silver cup of Polish soil; every mazurka and polonaise he wrote in Paris is Poland remembered at the piano.
dezerter: Dezerter formed in Warsaw under martial law in 1981 — Polish punk that dodged the censors with irony and became the scene's founding band.
daab: Daab brought reggae to 1980s Poland, where roots music about Babylon needed no translation.
basia: Basia took Polish jazz-pop worldwide from London — her late-80s hits like 'Time and Tide' made her one of the first Polish artists with US chart success.
abba: ABBA won Eurovision 1974 with 'Waterloo' and became the biggest pop export in Swedish history — the blueprint for Sweden's songwriting empire.
refused: Refused's 'The Shape of Punk to Come' (1998) — hardcore spliced with jazz and electronics from small-town Umeå — became one of punk's most influential records after the band had already broken up.
ebba gron: Ebba Grön were Swedish punk's founding trio (1977–83), snarling about the welfare state's cracks from the Stockholm suburb of Rågsved.
lisa ekdahl: Lisa Ekdahl sings jazz and bossa nova in a childlike Swedish-accented voice that made her a star in France as much as Sweden.
edvard grieg: Grieg built Norwegian national romanticism at the piano — 'Peer Gynt' and the Lyric Pieces carry Bergen's fjords into every concert hall.
grieg: Grieg built Norwegian national romanticism at the piano — 'Peer Gynt' and the Lyric Pieces carry Bergen's fjords into every concert hall.
a ha: a-ha's 'Take On Me' (1985) — that falsetto, that rotoscoped video — remains the biggest pop single ever to come out of Norway.
todd terje: Todd Terje is Oslo's nu-disco wit — 'Inspector Norse' (2012) made Norwegian space disco a global dancefloor language.
turbonegro: Turbonegro call their sound deathpunk — Oslo glam-punk provocateurs with denim, eyeliner and riffs borrowed from the Ramones and Alice Cooper alike.
miriam makeba: Miriam Makeba — Mama Africa — was exiled for three decades for singing against apartheid; 'Pata Pata' made her the first African woman with a global hit.
hugh masekela: Hugh Masekela fled apartheid with a trumpet Louis Armstrong helped send him, scored a US #1 with 'Grazing in the Grass', and sang the anti-apartheid anthem 'Bring Him Back Home'.
ladysmith black mambazo: Ladysmith Black Mambazo sing isicathamiya — the whisper-soft Zulu choral style born in miners' hostels — and carried it worldwide on Paul Simon's 'Graceland'.
brenda fassie: Brenda Fassie was 'the queen of African pop' — 'Weekend Special' (1983) defined bubblegum, township disco-pop at apartheid's height.
yvonne chaka chaka: Yvonne Chaka Chaka, 'the Princess of Africa', ruled 1980s bubblegum pop — 'Umqombothi' opened weddings and dancefloors across the continent.
ravi shankar: Ravi Shankar taught the West to hear the sitar — guru to George Harrison, headliner at Monterey and Woodstock, and still the reference point for Indian classical music abroad.
zakir hussain: Zakir Hussain is the tabla's global ambassador — son of the great Alla Rakha, collaborator of everyone from Shakti to the Grateful Dead's Mickey Hart.
lata mangeshkar: Lata Mangeshkar was Indian cinema's nightingale — the playback voice behind thousands of film songs across eight decades.
a r rahman: A.R. Rahman rewired Indian film music with synthesizers and Sufi soul from his Chennai studio — the 'Mozart of Madras' won two Oscars for 'Slumdog Millionaire'.
bts: BTS took K-pop from Seoul to the top of the Billboard Hot 100 — the biggest boy band of their era and Korea's loudest cultural export.
yellow magic orchestra: Yellow Magic Orchestra — Hosono, Sakamoto, Takahashi — were synth-pop prophets from 1978 Tokyo whose records seeded techno, hip hop and video game music alike.
pushim: Pushim is Japan's queen of reggae — an Osaka-born Zainichi Korean singer who made Japanese-language reggae a real scene.
mute beat: Mute Beat played trumpet-led dub in 1980s Tokyo clubs — the band that translated Kingston's echo chambers into Japanese and paved the way for the city's club culture.
antidoping: Antidoping have carried Mexican roots reggae from Mexico City since 1994 — proof the genre grew local roots far from Jamaica.
silvestre revueltas: Silvestre Revueltas wrote Mexico's revolution into orchestral music — 'Sensemayá' is Latin America's 'Rite of Spring'.
arturo marquez: Arturo Márquez's 'Danzón No. 2' — built on Veracruz ballroom rhythm — has become Mexico's unofficial second anthem in concert halls.
stan getz: Stan Getz's feather-toned tenor sax carried bossa nova into America — 'Getz/Gilberto' (1964) with João Gilberto and Jobim won Album of the Year and made 'The Girl from Ipanema' universal.
grupo fantasma: Grupo Fantasma are Austin's Latin-funk orchestra — a Grammy-winning border-sound big band that backed Prince himself.
